questions.st: A council is developing a web application that lets residents report potholes with a photo and a location. The application will be used on phones and desktop computers.

it.q: Explain why the application should use both client-side and server-side validation for the report form. (3 marks)
it.model: Client-side validation gives instant feedback, such as telling a resident that the location field is empty, so fewer incorrect forms are sent. It can be bypassed by disabling scripts or sending requests directly, so the server must validate every submission again before it is stored. Using both gives a quick user experience and protects the database.

2 marks: explains one type well and mentions the other.
1 mark: identifies validation with minimal explanation.

it.q: Outline TWO ways to reduce the time the pages take to load when residents upload photos. (3 marks)
it.model: Compress and resize photos in the browser before uploading, which reduces the amount of data sent. Use caching or a content delivery network so images and scripts that do not change are loaded from storage close to the user.
crit: Award up to 2 marks for two relevant ways and 1 mark for linking to load time.
Ways include: image compression, minifying CSS and JavaScript, caching, content delivery network, lazy loading, reducing the number of requests.

it.q: Describe ONE way the application can be tested to confirm it is accessible for residents with a vision impairment. (3 marks)
it.model: Test the pages with a screen reader. The tester checks that every photo has a text alternative, that form fields have labels that are read aloud, and that the whole form can be completed using only the keyboard. Any item that cannot be reached or understood is recorded and fixed.
crit: 3 marks: describes a specific test method and what is checked.

questions.st: A weather station operator enters the daily maximum temperature for each day. Entry stops when -999 is entered. At least one valid temperature is entered.

it.q: Using pseudocode, with a WHILE loop, write an algorithm to display the highest temperature entered and the number of days with a temperature above 35.
it.model:
BEGIN HeatRecord
    Set highest = -999
    Set hotDays = 0
    Get temp
    WHILE temp <> -999
        IF temp > highest THEN
            Set highest = temp
        ENDIF
        IF temp > 35 THEN
            Set hotDays = hotDays + 1
        ENDIF
        Get temp
    ENDWHILE
    Display "Highest: ", highest
    Display "Days above 35: ", hotDays
END HeatRecord
crit: 1 mark: correct loop that stops on -999 and reads input inside the loop (with an initial read before it).
1 mark: correctly finds the highest value and counts days above 35.
1 mark: initialises variables and displays both results after the loop.

it.q: Explain how hashing and salting help protect passwords stored in a database.
it.model: Hashing turns a password into a fixed-length value that cannot practically be reversed, so a stolen database does not reveal the passwords. A salt is a random value added to each password before hashing. It makes identical passwords produce different hashes and stops attackers using precomputed tables of common password hashes.
crit: 3 marks: explains hashing as one-way and salting as a unique random value, and links both to protection.
2 marks: explains one well and identifies the other.
1 mark: identifies hashing or salting with minimal explanation.

it.q: Describe how HTTPS (HTTP over TLS) protects data sent between a browser and a web server.
it.model: HTTPS uses TLS to set up an encrypted connection. The server proves its identity with a digital certificate, and the browser and server agree on session keys. Data sent after that is encrypted, so anyone intercepting it cannot read it, and changes to it can be detected.
crit: 3 marks: describes certificate or authentication, key exchange and encryption of data in transit.
2 marks: describes encryption with some detail about how it is set up.
1 mark: states that HTTPS encrypts data.

questions.st: A community library stores its members and loans in two related tables, Members and Loans.

it.q:
Construct a SQL query that displays, for each suburb, the number of loans that have a fine greater than 0.
Use the column headings Suburb and FinedLoans. List the results from the highest to the lowest number of fined loans.
it.model:
SELECT Suburb, COUNT(LoanID) AS FinedLoans
FROM Members
JOIN Loans ON Members.MemberID = Loans.MemberID
WHERE Fine > 0
GROUP BY Suburb
ORDER BY FinedLoans DESC
crit: 1 mark: selects Suburb and a count with the correct headings.

1 mark: filters to loans with Fine greater than 0.
1 mark: groups by Suburb and orders from highest to lowest.

questions.st: MediTime is a mobile app that a medical clinic is developing. Patients use it to book appointments and read their test results. Receptionists manage bookings. Doctors update patient records. The app stores personal health information in a cloud database and sends reminders by SMS.

it.q: Explain how the clinic can apply the principle of least privilege to protect patient records. (3 marks)
it.model: Each user receives only the access needed for their job. Patients can read only their own results, receptionists can change bookings but cannot open clinical notes, and only doctors can edit records. This limits the harm if an account is stolen and reduces accidental or deliberate misuse of patient data.

questions.st: A supermarket introduces self-service checkouts. A camera system uses computer vision to detect items that have not been scanned. When it detects a problem, it locks the checkout and alerts a staff member. Footage and alert data are stored to improve the system.

it.q: Discuss the social and ethical implications of this system for customers and staff.
it.model: Customers may feel watched and wrongly accused if the system makes a mistake, which damages trust and may unfairly affect people whose items are hard to recognise, such as shoppers with reusable bags. Footage is personal data, so the supermarket must store it securely, limit its use and tell customers about it. Staff may lose cashier jobs or be pushed into monitoring roles, which increases stress. Staff must also decide whether an alert is correct, so there should be a way for customers to challenge it. The system improves fairness by cutting theft, which can keep prices lower.
crit: 5 marks: a sustained discussion covering social and ethical implications for both customers and staff, supported by examples from the scenario.
3-4 marks: discusses several implications with some links to the scenario, or covers only one group well.
1-2 marks: identifies implications with limited explanation.
Ideas include: privacy and data security, false accusations and bias in detection, job change, human oversight, consent and transparency, benefits of reduced loss.

questions.st: A council introduces an artificial intelligence (AI) system to decide which road defects are repaired first. A neural network is trained on thousands of photos that engineers have labelled as pothole, crack or no defect. Residents can also submit photos through an app.

it.q: Explain how supervised learning is used to train the neural network for this system. Include ONE positive and ONE negative impact of using the system.
it.model: In supervised learning each training photo comes with a label from engineers. The network predicts a label, compares it with the correct one, and adjusts its weights to reduce the error, repeating this over many photos until it classifies new photos accurately. A positive impact is faster identification of dangerous potholes, so repairs reach the worst roads sooner. A negative impact is bias. If most training photos came from wealthy suburbs, the system may miss defects in other areas, so some residents wait longer for repairs.
crit: 5 marks: explains training with labelled data, prediction, error and adjustment, and gives one positive and one negative impact linked to the scenario.
3-4 marks: explains supervised learning with some detail and gives impacts with limited links.
1-2 marks: identifies supervised learning or one impact only.

questions.st: An employer uses an artificial intelligence (AI) tool to shortlist job applicants. The tool was trained on ten years of the company's past hiring decisions. A review finds that it rarely recommends applicants who have taken a career break. The company does not explain to applicants how the tool makes its decisions.

it.q: Evaluate the use of this tool. In your answer, refer to bias, transparency and human oversight.
it.model:
The tool can save time by sorting thousands of applications quickly and applying the same criteria to everyone, which can make early screening more consistent. However, it learned from past decisions. If earlier managers disadvantaged people with career breaks, the model has copied that pattern, so it scales the unfairness. Career breaks are common among carers and parents, so the result could discriminate against groups of people even though the tool never mentions them.
Because applicants are not told how the tool decides, they cannot challenge a rejection and the company cannot easily show that its process is fair. Lack of transparency also makes it harder to find the problem, which was only found because of a review.
Human oversight is needed. People should audit the outcomes regularly, remove the career-break feature and retrain on better data, and review borderline applications by hand. Overall the tool is useful only if bias is tested and decisions can be explained and appealed. Without those steps the risks to fairness and trust outweigh the time saved.
crit: 6 marks: a balanced evaluation that covers benefits and problems, explains bias, transparency and oversight with reference to the scenario, and reaches a justified judgement.
4-5 marks: explains most of the three areas with scenario links, with limited judgement.
2-3 marks: describes some issues with limited links to the scenario.
1 mark: identifies an issue only.

questions.st: A bike hire company charges $8 for the first hour and $5 for each extra hour. The cost for one day cannot be more than $40. The customer's hire time is a whole number of hours from 1 to 12.

it.q: Write an algorithm using pseudocode that gets the number of hours, calculates the cost and displays it. Include at least one subroutine in your answer.
it.model:
BEGIN BikeHire
    Get hours
    Set cost = CalculateCost(hours)
    Display "Hire cost: $", cost
END BikeHire

BEGIN CalculateCost(hours)
    Set cost = 8 + 5 * (hours - 1)
    IF cost > 40 THEN
        Set cost = 40
    ENDIF
    RETURN cost
END CalculateCost
crit: 1 mark: a subroutine with a parameter that returns or displays a value and is called from the main algorithm.
1 mark: correct calculation of $8 plus $5 for each extra hour.
1 mark: caps the cost at $40 and displays the result.

it.q: Explain how overfitting can be reduced when training a machine learning model.
it.model: Overfitting means learning training noise rather than general patterns. More varied, representative training data helps the model learn stable patterns. Regularisation penalises unnecessary complexity, while a simpler model has less capacity to memorise noise. A validation set or cross-validation detects poor generalisation; use those results to select model complexity or regularisation settings, or to guide early stopping. Testing alone does not change the model.
crit: 3 marks: explains at least two methods and links them to reducing memorisation of training data.
2 marks: explains one method well or two with limited detail.
1 mark: identifies one method.

it.q: Describe how a content delivery network (CDN) can reduce the load time of a website that is used around the world.
it.model: A CDN stores copies of a site's static files, such as images and scripts, on servers in many locations. When a user requests the page, the files come from the server nearest to them instead of the main server. The shorter distance reduces delay, and spreading requests across servers reduces the load on the main server.

questions.st: GreenCart is an online store that sells reusable household products. It is preparing a flash sale in which thousands of customers will buy limited stock in a short time. The store accepts card payments, keeps customer accounts and lets customers write product reviews.

it.q: Describe how static application security testing (SAST) and dynamic application security testing (DAST) can be used at different stages of developing GreenCart. (3 marks)
it.model: SAST analyses the source code without running it, so it can be used while the code is being written, for example to find a query built from unchecked input. it.q: Evaluate the THREE proposals and recommend the most suitable one for the council.
it.model: Proposal A reduces the risk of another card-data loss by removing stored card numbers from the council app. Developer training and scanning every change can prevent or identify vulnerabilities during development. However, scanning cannot guarantee that all flaws are found, and the council must rely on the payment provider. Proposal B has the stated lowest cost and four-week delivery. A web application firewall can block some malicious requests, while encryption helps protect stored data. However, these controls do not establish that flaws in the existing code have been corrected; compromise of the running app or encryption keys could still expose card data. Proposal C improves detection and account protection through monitoring and multi-factor authentication, and independent penetration tests can reveal weaknesses. However, annual testing may leave gaps between tests, and the proposal does not state that card storage will end or that identified flaws will be repaired. A is recommended because it directly reduces the stored data exposed in a future breach and integrates preventive checks into development. The cause of the original attack and A’s cost and delivery time are not given, so these cannot be assumed.
